entities.summary:
Lu Ban, a legendary master craftsman and inventor of the Spring and Autumn period (771–476 BCE) of ancient China, stands as a foundational figure in the history of East Asian technology and engineering. Born in the state of Lu, likely in modern-day Shandong province, his life, though shrouded in apocryphal tales, represents the zenith of practical ingenuity during a transformative era of societal development and escalating warfare. Revered posthumously as the patron deity of carpenters, masons, and architects, his contributions fundamentally shaped construction techniques, military siegecraft, and everyday tool design across the Chinese cultural sphere for millennia. His death, recorded around 443 BCE, marks the transition from the Spring and Autumn period into the Warring States period, an era where his innovations would find even greater application.

Attributed to Lu Ban are a remarkable array of inventions that revolutionized ancient Chinese construction and warfare. Among his most celebrated innovations are the cloud ladder (a mobile siege tower), the grappling hook and ram, and the wooden horse and carriage, an early form of self-propelled vehicle. In carpentry, he is credited with developing the plane, the ink line (mozi), and various types of saws and drills, tools that became indispensable for precise woodworking. These advancements allowed for the construction of more sophisticated buildings, from palaces to fortifications, and significantly impacted military logistics and assault capabilities during a period of intense interstate conflict.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Lu Ban's legendary inventions, particularly in carpentry and siegecraft, fundamentally advanced ancient Chinese technology, influencing construction and warfare for millennia. His deification as a patron deity underscores his enduring cultural and practical impact on East Asian craftsmanship.
